canonical_policy.name: API deprecation preserves the promised migration window
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: When deprecating an externally consumed API version, mark the deprecation in versioning metadata, document the replacement, communicate a realistic migration/removal timeline, and keep the old version working for the promised support period; do not remove it without considering the published support contract.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Deprecation metadata/replacement/timeline/support period match; meaningful coexistence tests alreadyEXTRA0066. No absolute never-remove-after-promise inference.

context_quotes: When versions coexist, test meaningful differences: version routing, version-specific response shapes, a deprecated version still operating during its support period, unsupported-version behavior, shared Application behavior staying consistent. Identical behavior needs no duplicated tests per version.

- Classify the change as compatible or breaking (technique: `api-versioning`); a breaking change to a relied-on contract follows `rules/backend/api.md` § Versioning; it is Reserved.
- Deprecating an externally consumed API version: mark the deprecation in versioning metadata, document the replacement version, communicate a realistic migration and removal timeline, and keep the old version working for the promised support period. Do not remove a deprecated version without considering its published support contract.

canonical_policy.name: Protect sensitive transport
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Production traffic carrying credentials or sensitive data must use TLS; respect actual hosting topology and never disable certificate validation to make integration work.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Sensitive Production TLS and no certificate bypass match; external termination/in-app redirect exception retained. Local exampleTrustServerCertificate alreadyBF0002.

context_quotes:
- Production traffic carrying credentials or sensitive data must use TLS. Respect the actual hosting topology: TLS may terminate in the application, a reverse proxy, ingress controller, gateway or hosting platform, and in-app HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection is not required when the deployment already provides the secure transport boundary.
- Never disable certificate validation to make an integration work.

Rules: `rules/common/security.md` § Transport security. Review disabled certificate validation, accept-all certificate callbacks and plain HTTP for sensitive external communication, accounting for TLS termination at proxies, ingress, gateways or the hosting platform. Missing in-app HTTPS redirection is not automatically a vulnerability.

4. Do not suppress a real secret because it sits in a Development file.
5. Do not require security mechanisms the project does not need.
6. Evaluate effective authorization behavior, including global and fallback policies.

Not automatically vulnerabilities: an endpoint without `[Authorize]` protected by a secure fallback policy; bare `[Authorize]` when authentication alone is intended; `AllowAnyOrigin()` on a genuinely public, non-credentialed API; MD5/SHA1 as a non-security checksum; no application-level encryption when platform or storage encryption satisfies the requirement; obviously fake test credentials; framework defaults that are secure in the actual hosting configuration.

Recommend the smallest secure change consistent with the project architecture. Do not recommend a new authentication system unnecessarily, custom cryptography, blanket encryption of all database fields, `[Authorize]` on every action when a global policy already protects them, security libraries merely to satisfy the scan, or disabling functionality because a static scanner cannot understand it.

Flag security-sensitive use of MD5, SHA1, ECB mode, hardcoded encryption keys, custom password hashing and home-grown encryption protocols — but not MD5/SHA1 used as non-security checksums. Passwords use established password-hashing facilities (ASP.NET Core Identity password hashers), not reversible encryption.

Match protection to the requirement: passwords → one-way password hashing; verification-only tokens → often hashed rather than reversibly encrypted; retrievable application secrets → protected/encrypted storage; database/storage encryption → platform or database mechanism when suitable; temporary application payloads → ASP.NET Core Data Protection may fit.

canonical_policy.name: CORS is least-permissive for requirements
